{{short description|Statistical method}}
{{About|statistics and machine learning|other uses|Lasso (disambiguation)}}

In [[statistics]] and [[machine learning]], '''lasso''' ('''least absolute shrinkage and selection operator'''; also '''Lasso''', '''LASSO''' or '''L1 regularization''')<ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=18 January 2024 |title=What is lasso regression? |url=https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/lasso-regression |website=[[ibm.com]]|access-date=4 January 2025}}</ref> is a [[regression analysis]] method that performs both [[variable selection]] and [[Regularization (mathematics)|regularization]] in order to enhance the prediction accuracy and interpretability of the resulting [[statistical model]]. The lasso method assumes that the coefficients of the linear model are sparse, meaning that few of them are non-zero. It was originally introduced in [[geophysics]],<ref name="Breiman 1995">{{cite journal|last1=Santosa|first1=Fadil|last2=Symes|first2=William W.|year=1986|title=Linear inversion of band-limited reflection seismograms.|journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific and Statistical Computing|publisher=SIAM|volume=7|issue=4|pages=1307–1330|doi=10.1137/0907087}}</ref> and later by [[Robert Tibshirani]],<ref name = "Tibshirani 1996">{{cite journal |last=Tibshirani |first=Robert |year=1996 |title=Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the lasso |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |series=Series B (methodological) |volume=58 |issue=1 |publisher=Wiley |pages=267–88 |doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1996.tb02080.x |jstor=2346178 }}</ref> who coined the term.

Lasso was originally formulated for [[linear regression]] models. This simple case reveals a substantial amount about the estimator. These include its relationship to [[ridge regression]] and [[best subset selection]] and the connections between lasso coefficient estimates and so-called soft thresholding. It also reveals that (like standard linear regression) the coefficient estimates do not need to be unique if [[covariate]]s are [[collinear]].

Though originally defined for linear regression, lasso regularization is easily extended to other statistical models including [[generalized linear model]]s, [[generalized estimating equation]]s, [[proportional hazards model]]s, and [[M-estimator]]s.<ref name="Tibshirani 1996" /><ref name="Tibshirani 1997">{{cite journal |last=Tibshirani |first=Robert |title=The lasso Method for Variable Selection in the Cox Model |journal=[[Statistics in Medicine (journal)|Statistics in Medicine]] |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=385–395 |year=1997 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19970228)16:4<385::AID-SIM380>3.0.CO;2-3 |pmid=9044528 |citeseerx=10.1.1.411.8024 }}</ref> Lasso's ability to perform subset selection relies on the form of the constraint and has a variety of interpretations including in terms of [[geometry]], [[Bayesian statistics]] and [[convex analysis]].

The LASSO is closely related to [[basis pursuit denoising]].

== History ==
Lasso was introduced in order to improve the prediction accuracy and interpretability of regression models. It selects a reduced set of the known covariates for use in a model.<ref name = "Tibshirani 1996" /><ref name="Breiman 1995"/>

Lasso was developed independently in geophysics literature in 1986, based on prior work that used the [[L1 norm|<math>\ell^1</math>]] [[Penalized least squares|penalty]] for both fitting and penalization of the coefficients. Statistician [[Robert Tibshirani]] independently rediscovered and popularized it in 1996, based on [[Leo Breiman|Breiman]]'s nonnegative garrote.<ref name="Breiman 1995" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Breiman|first=Leo|title=Better Subset Regression Using the Nonnegative Garrote|journal=Technometrics|volume=37|issue=4|pages=373–84|doi=10.1080/00401706.1995.10484371|year=1995}}</ref>

Prior to lasso, the most widely used method for choosing covariates was [[Stepwise regression|stepwise selection]]. That approach only improves prediction accuracy in certain cases, such as when only a few covariates have a strong relationship with the outcome. However, in other cases, it can increase prediction error.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=1707.08692 |last1=Hastie |first1=Trevor |last2=Tibshirani |first2=Robert |last3=Tibshirani |first3=Ryan J. |title=Extended Comparisons of Best Subset Selection, Forward Stepwise Selection, and the Lasso |date=2017 |class=stat.ME }}</ref>

At the time, [[Tikhonov regularization|ridge regression]] was the most popular technique for improving prediction accuracy. Ridge regression improves prediction error by [[Shrinkage (statistics)|shrinking]] the sum of the squares of the [[regression coefficients]] to be less than a fixed value in order to reduce [[overfitting]], but it does not perform covariate selection and therefore does not help to make the model more interpretable.

Lasso achieves both of these goals by forcing the sum of the [[absolute value]] of the regression coefficients to be less than a fixed value, which forces certain coefficients to zero, excluding them from impacting prediction. This idea is similar to ridge regression, which also shrinks the size of the coefficients; however, ridge regression does not set coefficients to zero (and, thus, does not perform [[variable selection]]).

== Basic form ==

=== Least squares ===
Consider a sample consisting of ''N'' cases, each of which consists of ''p'' [[covariate]]s and a single outcome. Let <math> y_i </math> be the outcome and <math> x_i:=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_p)_i^\intercal</math> be the covariate vector for the ''i'' <sup>th</sup> case. Then the objective of lasso is to solve:<ref name="Tibshirani 1996" />
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta_0, \beta } \biggl\{ \sum_{i=1}^N \bigl(y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\intercal \beta\bigr)^2 \biggr\} </math>
subject to
<math display="block"> \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j| \leq t. </math>

Here <math> \beta_0 </math> is the constant coefficient, <math> \beta:=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\ldots, \beta_p)</math> is the coefficient vector, and <math>t</math> is a prespecified [[free parameter]] that determines the degree of regularization.

Letting <math> X </math> be the covariate matrix, so that <math> X_{ij} = (x_i)_j </math> and <math>x_i^\intercal</math> is the ''i'' <sup>th</sup> row of <math>X</math>, the expression can be written more compactly as
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta_0, \beta } \left\{ \left\| y - \beta_0  - X \beta \right\|_2^2 \right\} \text{ subject to } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t, </math>
where <math> \| u \|_p = \biggl( \sum_{i=1}^N | u_i |^p \biggr)^{1/p} </math> is the standard [[Lp space#The p-norm in finite dimensions|<math> \ell^p </math> norm]].

Denoting the scalar mean of the data points <math>x_i</math> by <math>\bar{x}</math> and the mean of the response variables <math>y_i</math> by <math>\bar{y}</math>, the resulting estimate for <math>\beta_0</math> is <math> \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \bar{x}^\intercal \beta </math>, so that
<math display="block"> y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - x_i^\intercal \beta = y_i - ( \bar{y} - \bar{x}^\intercal \beta ) - x_i^\intercal \beta = ( y_i - \bar{y} ) - ( x_i - \bar{x} )^\intercal \beta, </math>
and therefore it is standard to work with variables that have been made zero-mean. Additionally, the covariates are typically [[Standardized (statistics)|standardized]] <math display="inline"> \bigl( \sum_{i=1}^N x_{i}^2 = 1 \bigr) </math> so that the solution does not depend on the measurement scale.

It can be helpful to rewrite
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| y - X \beta \right\|_2^2 \right\} \text{ subject to } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t. </math>
in the so-called [[Lagrange multiplier|Lagrangian]] form
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| y - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|_1 \right\} </math>
where the exact relationship between <math> t </math> and <math> \lambda </math> is data dependent.

=== Orthonormal covariates ===

Some basic properties of the lasso estimator can now be considered.

Assuming first that the covariates are [[orthonormal]] so that <math>\ x_i^\intercal x_j = \delta_{ij}\ ,</math> where <math>\ \delta_{ij}\ </math> is the [[Kronecker delta]], or, equivalently, <math>\ X^\intercal X = I\ ,</math> then using [[subgradient methods]] it can be shown that<ref name = "Tibshirani 1996"/>
<math display="block">
\,\begin{align}
\hat{\beta}_j\ =\ {} & \operatorname{S}_{N, \lambda}\left(\hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} \right)\ =\ \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} \cdot \max\! \left\{\ 0,\ 1 - \frac{\ N\ \lambda\ }{\ \bigl|\hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}}\bigr|\ }\ \right\} \end{align}\,</math>

where 
<math>\quad \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}}\ =\ (X^\intercal X)^{-1} X^\intercal y\ =\ X^\intercal y ~.
</math>

<math>\ S_\alpha\ </math> is referred to as the ''soft thresholding operator'', since it translates values towards zero (making them exactly zero in the limit as they themselves approach zero) instead of setting smaller values to zero and leaving larger ones untouched as the ''hard thresholding operator'', often denoted <math>\ H_\alpha\ ,</math> would.

In ridge regression the objective is to minimize
<math display="block">\ \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{~ \tfrac{\ 1\ }{ N } \Bigl\|\ y - X\ \beta\ \Bigr\|_2^2\ +\ \lambda\ \Bigl\|\ \beta\ \Bigr\|_2^2 ~\right\}\ </math>

Using <math>\ X^\intercal X = I\ </math> and the ridge regression formula: <math>\ \hat{\beta} = \Bigl(\ X^\intercal X\ +\ N\ \lambda\ I\ \Bigr)^{-1} X^\intercal y\ ,</math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=McDonald |first1=Gary |title=Ridge regression |journal=Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Computational Statistics |year=2009 |volume=1 |pages=93–100 |doi=10.1002/wics.14 |s2cid=64699223 |url=https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/wics.14 |access-date=August 22, 2022 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> yields:
<math display="block">\ \hat{\beta}_j = \left( 1 + N\ \lambda \right)^{-1}\ \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} ~.</math>

Ridge regression shrinks all coefficients by a uniform factor of <math>\ (1 + N \lambda)^{-1}\ </math> and does not set any coefficients to zero.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Melkumova |first1=L.E. |last2=Shatskikh |first2=S.Ya. |date=2017-01-01 |title=Comparing Ridge and LASSO estimators for data analysis |journal=Procedia Engineering |series=3rd International Conference “Information Technology and Nanotechnology", ITNT-2017, 25–27 April 2017, Samara, Russia |volume=201 |pages=746–755 |doi=10.1016/j.proeng.2017.09.615 |issn=1877-7058|doi-access=free }}</ref>

It can also be compared to regression with [[best subset selection]], in which the goal is to minimize
<math display="block">\ \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{~ \tfrac{1}{N} \Bigl\|\ y - X \beta\ \Bigr\|_2^2\ +\ \lambda\ \Bigl\|\ \beta\ \Bigr\|_0 ~\right\}\ </math>
where <math>\ \| \cdot \|_0\ </math> is the "<math>\ \ell^0\ </math> norm", which is defined as <math>\ \| z \| = m\ </math> if exactly {{mvar|m}} components of {{mvar|z}} are nonzero. Again assuming orthonormal covariates, it can be shown that in this special case
<math display="block">\ \hat{\beta}_j\ =\ H_{ \sqrt{ N \lambda\ } }\ \left(\ \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}}\ \right)\ =\ \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} \cdot \operatorname\mathbb{I} \left[~ \bigl| \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} \bigr| \geq \sqrt{ N\ \lambda\ } ~\right]\ </math>
where <math>\ H_\alpha\ </math> is again the hard thresholding operator and <math>\ \mathbb{I}\ </math> is an [[indicator function]] (it is {{math|1}} if its argument is true and {{math|0}} otherwise).

Therefore, the lasso estimates share features of both ridge and best subset selection regression since they both shrink the magnitude of all the coefficients, like ridge regression and set some of them to zero, as in the best subset selection case. Additionally, while ridge regression scales all of the coefficients by a constant factor, lasso instead translates the coefficients towards zero by a constant value and sets them to zero if they reach it.

=== Correlated covariates ===

In one special case two covariates, say ''j'' and ''k'', are identical for each observation, so that <math> x_{(j)} = x_{(k)} </math>, where <math> x_{(j),i} = x_{(k),i} </math>. Then the values of <math> \beta_j </math> and <math> \beta_k </math> that minimize the lasso objective function are not uniquely determined. In fact, if some <math> \hat{\beta} </math> in which <math> \hat{\beta}_j \hat{\beta}_k \geq 0 </math>, then if <math> s \in [0,1] </math> replacing <math> \hat{\beta}_j </math> by <math> s ( \hat{\beta}_j + \hat{\beta}_k ) </math> and <math> \hat{\beta}_k </math> by <math> (1 - s ) ( \hat{\beta}_j + \hat{\beta}_k ) </math>, while keeping all the other <math> \hat{\beta}_i </math> fixed, gives a new solution, so the lasso objective function then has a continuum of valid minimizers.<ref name = "Zou 2005" /> Several variants of the lasso, including the [[Elastic net regularization]], have been designed to address this shortcoming.

== General form ==

Lasso regularization can be extended to other objective functions such as those for [[generalized linear model]]s, [[generalized estimating equation]]s, [[proportional hazards model]]s, and [[M-estimator]]s.<ref name = "Tibshirani 1996" /><ref name = "Tibshirani 1997" /> Given the objective function
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N f( x_i, y_i, \alpha, \beta ) </math>
the lasso regularized version of the estimator ''s'' the solution to
<math display="block"> \min_{ \alpha, \beta } \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N f( x_i, y_i, \alpha, \beta ) \text{ subject to } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t </math>
where only <math> \beta </math> is penalized while <math> \alpha </math> is free to take any allowed value, just as <math> \beta_0 </math> was not penalized in the basic case.

== <span class="anchor" id="Interpretations of lasso"></span>Interpretations ==

=== Geometric interpretation ===
[[Image:L1_and_L2_balls.svg|300px|thumb|Forms of the constraint regions for lasso and ridge regression]]

Lasso can set coefficients to zero, while the superficially similar ridge regression cannot. This is due to the difference in the shape of their constraint boundaries. Both lasso and ridge regression can be interpreted as minimizing the same objective function
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta_0, \beta } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| y - \beta_0 - X \beta \right\|_2^2 \right\} </math>
but with respect to different constraints: <math> \| \beta \|_1 \leq t </math> for lasso and <math> \| \beta \|_2^2 \leq t </math> for ridge. The figure shows that the constraint region defined by the <math> \ell^1 </math> norm is a square rotated so that its corners lie on the axes (in general a [[cross-polytope]]), while the region defined by the <math> \ell^2 </math> norm is a circle (in general an [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]]), which is [[Rotation (mathematics)|rotationally]] [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] and, therefore, has no corners. As seen in the figure, a convex object that lies tangent to the boundary, such as the line shown, is likely to encounter a corner (or a higher-dimensional equivalent) of a hypercube, for which some components of <math> \beta </math> are identically zero, while in the case of an ''n''-sphere, the points on the boundary for which some of the components of <math> \beta </math> are zero are not distinguished from the others and the convex object is no more likely to contact a point at which some components of <math> \beta </math> are zero than one for which none of them are.

=== Making λ easier to interpret with an accuracy-simplicity tradeoff ===

The lasso can be rescaled so that it becomes easy to anticipate and influence the degree of shrinkage associated with a given value of <math> \lambda </math>.<ref name="Hoornweg2018SUS">{{cite book |last1=Hoornweg |first1=Victor |title=Science: Under Submission | chapter=Chapter 8 | date=2018 |publisher=Hoornweg Press |isbn=978-90-829188-0-9 |chapter-url=http://www.victorhoornweg.com}}</ref> It is assumed that <math>X</math> is standardized with z-scores and that <math>y</math> is centered (zero mean). Let <math>\beta_0</math> represent the hypothesized regression coefficients and let <math>b_\text{OLS}</math> refer to the data-optimized ordinary least squares solutions. We can then define the [[Lagrange multiplier|Lagrangian]] as a tradeoff between the in-sample accuracy of the data-optimized solutions and the simplicity of sticking to the hypothesized values.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Motamedi |first1=Fahimeh  |last2=Sanchez |first2=Horacio |last3=Mehri |first3=Alireza |last4=Ghasemi |first4=Fahimeh |title= Accelerating Big Data Analysis through LASSO-Random Forest Algorithm in QSAR Studies|journal=Bioinformatics | volume = 37 | issue = 19 | pages = 469–475 | date =  October 2021 | issn = 1367-4803 |doi= 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab659 |pmid=34979024 }}</ref> This results in
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } 
\left\{ 
  \frac{(y-X\beta)'(y-X\beta)}{(y-X\beta_0)'(y-X\beta_0)} + 2\lambda \sum_{i=1}^p  \frac{|\beta_i-\beta_{0,i}|}{q_{i}}
\right\} 
</math>
where <math> q_i </math> is specified below and the "prime" symbol stands for transpose. The first fraction represents relative accuracy, the second fraction relative simplicity, and <math>\lambda</math> balances between the two.

[[File:SolutionPathL1L2.svg|thumb|Solution paths for the <math>\ell_1</math> norm and <math>\ell_2</math> norm when <math>b_\text{OLS}=2</math> and <math>\beta_{0}=0</math>]]
Given a single regressor, relative simplicity can be defined by specifying <math>q_i</math> as <math>|b_\text{OLS}-\beta_{0}|</math>, which is the maximum amount of deviation from <math>\beta_0</math> when <math> \lambda=0 </math>. Assuming that <math>\beta_{0}=0</math>, the solution path can be defined in terms of [[coefficient of determination|<math>R^2</math>]]:
<math display="block">
b_{\ell_1} = \begin{cases}
(1-\lambda/R^{2})b_\text{OLS}          &  \mbox{if } \lambda \leq R^{2}, \\ 
0                  &  \mbox{if } \lambda>R^{2}.
\end{cases}
</math>
If <math>\lambda=0</math>, the ordinary least squares solution (OLS) is used. The hypothesized value of <math>\beta_0=0</math> is selected if <math>\lambda</math> is bigger than <math>R^2</math>. Furthermore, if <math>R^2=1</math>, then <math>\lambda</math> represents the proportional influence of <math>\beta_0=0</math>. In other words, <math>\lambda\times100\%</math> measures in percentage terms the minimal amount of influence of the hypothesized value relative to the data-optimized OLS solution.

If an <math>\ell_2</math>-norm is used to penalize deviations from zero given a single regressor, the solution path is given by
<math display="block">b_{\ell_2} = \left(1+\frac{\lambda}{R^{2}(1-\lambda)}\right)^{-1} b_\text{OLS}.</math>
Like <math>b_{\ell_1}</math>, <math>b_{\ell_2}</math> moves in the direction of the point <math>(\lambda = R^2, b=0)</math> when <math>\lambda</math> is close to zero; but unlike <math>b_{\ell_1}</math>, the influence of <math>R^2</math> diminishes in <math>b_{\ell_2}</math> if <math>\lambda</math> increases (see figure). <br/>Given multiple regressors, the moment that a parameter is activated (i.e. allowed to deviate from <math>\beta_0</math>) is also determined by a regressor's contribution to <math>R^2</math> accuracy. First, 
<math display="block">R^2=1-\frac{(y-Xb)'(y-Xb)}{(y-X\beta_0)'(y-X\beta_0)}.</math>
An <math>R^2</math> of 75% means that in-sample accuracy improves by 75% if the unrestricted OLS solutions are used instead of the hypothesized <math>\beta_0</math> values. The individual contribution of deviating from each hypothesis can be computed with the <math>p</math> x <math>p</math> matrix 
<math display="block">R^{\otimes}=(X'\tilde y_0)(X'\tilde y_0)' (X'X)^{-1}(\tilde y_0'\tilde y_0)^{-1},</math>
where <math>\tilde y_0=y-X\beta_0</math>. If <math>b=b_\text{OLS}</math> when <math>R^2</math> is computed, then the diagonal elements of <math>R^{\otimes}</math> sum to <math>R^2</math>. The diagonal <math>R^{\otimes}</math> values may be smaller than 0 or, less often, larger than 1. If regressors are uncorrelated, then the <math>i^{th}</math> diagonal element of <math>R^{\otimes}</math> simply corresponds to the <math>r^2</math> value between <math>x_i</math> and <math>y</math>.

A rescaled version of the adaptive lasso of can be obtained by setting <math>q_{\mbox{adaptive lasso},i}=|b_{\text{OLS},i}-\beta_{0,i}|</math>.<ref name="Zou2006">{{cite web|last=Zou |first=Hui |year=2006 |url=http://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~shao/stat992/zou2006.pdf |title= The Adaptive Lasso and Its Oracle Properties}}</ref> If regressors are uncorrelated, the moment that the <math>i^{th}</math> parameter is activated is given by the <math>i^{th}</math> diagonal element of <math>R^{\otimes}</math>. Assuming for convenience that <math>\beta_0</math> is a vector of zeros,
<math display="block"> b_{i} = \begin{cases}
 (1-\lambda/R_{ii}^{\otimes})b_{\text{OLS},i} & \text{if } \lambda \leq R_{ii}^{\otimes}, \\ 
 0                                            & \text{if } \lambda    > R_{ii}^{\otimes}.
 \end{cases}
</math>
That is, if regressors are uncorrelated, <math>\lambda</math> again specifies the minimal influence of <math>\beta_0</math>. Even when regressors are correlated, the first time that a regression parameter is activated occurs when <math>\lambda</math> is equal to the highest diagonal element of <math>R^{\otimes}</math>.

These results can be compared to a rescaled version of the lasso by defining <math>q_{\mbox{lasso},i}=\frac{1}{p} \sum_{l} |b_{\text{OLS},l}-\beta_{0,l}|</math>, which is the average absolute deviation of <math>b_\text{OLS}</math> from <math>\beta_0</math>. Assuming that regressors are uncorrelated, then the moment of activation of the <math>i^{th}</math> regressor is given by
<math display="block"> \tilde \lambda_{\text{lasso},i} = \frac{1}{p}\sqrt{R^{\otimes}_i} \sum_{l=1}^p\sqrt{R^{\otimes}_{l}}.</math>

For <math>p=1</math>, the moment of activation is again given by <math>\tilde \lambda_{\text{lasso},i}=R^2</math>. If <math>\beta_0</math> is a vector of zeros and a subset of <math>p_B</math> relevant parameters are equally responsible for a perfect fit of <math>R^2=1</math>, then this subset is activated at a <math>\lambda</math> value of <math>\frac{1}{p}</math>. The moment of activation of a relevant regressor then equals <math>\frac{1}{p}\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_B}}p_B\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_B}}=\frac{1}{p}</math>. In other words, the inclusion of irrelevant regressors delays the moment that relevant regressors are activated by this rescaled lasso. The adaptive lasso and the lasso are special cases of a '1ASTc' estimator. The latter only groups parameters together if the absolute correlation among regressors is larger than a user-specified value.<ref name = "Hoornweg2018SUS" />

=== Bayesian interpretation ===

[[Image:Laplace_pdf_mod.svg|thumb|Laplace distributions are sharply peaked at their mean with more probability density concentrated there compared to a normal distribution.]]

Just as ridge regression can be interpreted as linear regression for which the coefficients have been assigned normal [[prior distribution]]s, lasso can be interpreted as linear regression for which the coefficients have [[Laplace distribution|Laplace prior distributions]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Huang | first1 = Yunfei. | display-authors = etal | year = 2022 | title = Sparse inference and active learning of stochastic differential equations from data | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 12 | number = 1| article-number = 21691 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-022-25638-9  | pmid = 36522347 | doi-access = free| pmc = 9755218 | arxiv = 2203.11010 | bibcode = 2022NatSR..1221691H }}</ref> The Laplace distribution is sharply [[Peakedness|peaked]] at zero (its first derivative is discontinuous at zero) and it concentrates its probability mass closer to zero than does the [[normal distribution]]. This provides an alternative explanation of why lasso tends to set some coefficients to zero, while ridge regression does not.<ref name = "Tibshirani 1996" />

=== Convex relaxation interpretation ===

Lasso can also be viewed as a convex relaxation of the best subset selection regression problem, which is to find the subset of <math> \leq k </math> covariates that results in the smallest value of the objective function for some fixed <math> k \leq n </math>, where n is the total number of covariates. The "<math> \ell^0 </math> norm", <math> \|  \cdot \|_0 </math>, (the number of nonzero entries of a vector), is the limiting case of "<math>\ell^p </math> norms", of the form <math> \textstyle \| x \|_p = \left( \sum_{i=1}^n | x_j |^p \right)^{1/p} </math> (where the quotation marks signify that these are not really norms for <math> p < 1 </math> since <math> \| \cdot \|_p </math> is not convex for <math> p < 1 </math>, so the triangle inequality does not hold). Therefore, since p = 1 is the smallest value for which the "<math> \ell^p </math> norm" is convex (and therefore actually a norm), lasso is, in some sense, the best convex approximation to the best subset selection problem, since the region defined by <math> \| x \|_1 \leq t </math> is the [[convex hull]] of the region defined by <math> \| x \|_p \leq t </math> for <math> p < 1 </math>.

== Prediction error guarantees ==

Theoretical guarantees for the lasso include bounds on its prediction error in high-dimensional regression, where the number of covariates can exceed the sample size. For a fixed design matrix <math>X</math>, consider the linear model <math>y=X\beta^\star+\varepsilon</math>, with <math>n</math> observations, <math>p</math> covariates and independent Gaussian errors of variance <math>\sigma^2</math>. Bickel, Ritov and Tsybakov established prediction-error bounds under a restricted eigenvalue condition on the design matrix. If <math>\beta^\star</math> has at most <math>s</math> nonzero coefficients, the columns of <math>X</math> are normalized and the regularization parameter is suitably chosen, their results give, with high probability,
:<math>\frac{1}{n}\left\|X(\widehat{\beta}-\beta^\star)\right\|_2^2 \leq C\frac{\sigma^2 s\log p}{n},</math>
where <math>C</math> depends on the restricted eigenvalue bound and the tuning constant. The restricted eigenvalue condition controls the design matrix on a restricted set of coefficient directions and does not require <math>X^\mathsf{T}X</math> to be invertible.<ref name="BRT2009">{{cite journal |last1=Bickel |first1=Peter J. |last2=Ritov |first2=Ya'acov |last3=Tsybakov |first3=Alexandre B. |title=Simultaneous analysis of Lasso and Dantzig selector |journal=The Annals of Statistics |year=2009 |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=1705–1732 |doi=10.1214/08-AOS620 |arxiv=0801.1095}}</ref>

Prediction guarantees can also take the form of ''oracle inequalities'', which compare the lasso's error with the approximation error of a sparse linear predictor plus a term accounting for estimation error. Koltchinskii, Lounici and Tsybakov proved a sharp oracle inequality for the fixed-design lasso under a restricted eigenvalue condition. Here, ''sharp'' means that the coefficient multiplying the approximation-error term is exactly one. Their bound therefore allows comparison with sparse approximations even when the underlying coefficient vector is not itself sparse.<ref name="KLT2011">{{cite journal |last1=Koltchinskii |first1=Vladimir |last2=Lounici |first2=Karim |last3=Tsybakov |first3=Alexandre B. |title=Nuclear-norm penalization and optimal rates for noisy low-rank matrix completion |journal=The Annals of Statistics |year=2011 |volume=39 |issue=5 |doi=10.1214/11-AOS894 |arxiv=1011.6256}}</ref>

For random designs, prediction on new observations is measured by an error averaged over the distribution of the covariates, rather than only over the observed design points. Bellec, Dalalyan, Grappin and Paris studied adaptations of the lasso to semi-supervised and transductive learning, in which additional covariate observations are available without response labels. Under boundedness and appropriate design conditions, they established oracle inequalities both with high probability and in expectation. Their analysis shows how unlabeled observations can improve estimation of the covariate covariance matrix and relax the conditions needed for fast prediction rates. The paper also reviews earlier results on prediction error for the lasso with random designs.<ref name="BDGP2018">{{cite journal |last1=Bellec |first1=Pierre C. |last2=Dalalyan |first2=Arnak S. |last3=Grappin |first3=Edwin |last4=Paris |first4=Quentin |title=On the prediction loss of the lasso in the partially labeled setting |journal=Electronic Journal of Statistics |year=2018 |volume=12 |issue=2 |doi=10.1214/18-EJS1457 |arxiv=1606.06179}}</ref>

== Generalizations ==

Lasso variants have been created in order to remedy limitations of the original technique and to make the method more useful for particular problems. Almost all of these focus on respecting or exploiting dependencies among the covariates.

[[Elastic net regularization]] adds an additional ridge regression-like penalty that improves performance when the number of predictors is larger than the sample size, allows the method to select strongly correlated variables together, and improves overall prediction accuracy.<ref name="Zou 2005">{{cite journal |last1=Zou |first1=Hui |first2=Trevor |last2=Hastie |year=2005 |title=Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |series=Series B (statistical Methodology) |volume=67 |issue=2 |publisher=Wiley |pages=301–20 |jstor=3647580 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9868.2005.00503.x |s2cid=122419596 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Group lasso allows groups of related covariates to be selected as a single unit, which can be useful in settings where it does not make sense to include some covariates without others.<ref name="Yuan 2006">{{cite journal |last1=Yuan |first1=Ming |first2=Yi |last2=Lin |year=2006 |title=Model Selection and Estimation in Regression with Grouped Variables |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |series=Series B (statistical Methodology) |volume=68 |issue=1 |publisher=Wiley |pages=49–67 |jstor=3647556 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9868.2005.00532.x |s2cid=6162124 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Further extensions of group lasso perform variable selection within individual groups (sparse group lasso) and allow overlap between groups (overlap group lasso).<ref name="Puig 2009">Puig, Arnau Tibau, Ami Wiesel, and [[Alfred O. Hero III]]. "[https://hal-supelec.archives-ouvertes.fr/docs/00/44/42/55/PDF/Arnau_TIBAU.pdf A Multidimensional Shrinkage-Thresholding Operator]". Proceedings of the 15th workshop on Statistical Signal Processing, SSP'09, IEEE, pp. 113–116.</ref><ref name="Jacob 2009">Jacob, Laurent, Guillaume Obozinski, and Jean-Philippe Vert. "[http://videolectures.net/site/normal_dl/tag=48041/icml09_jacob_glog_01.pdf Group Lasso with Overlap and Graph LASSO]". Appearing in Proceedings of the 26th International Conference on Machine Learning, Montreal, Canada, 2009.</ref>

Fused lasso can account for the spatial or temporal characteristics of a problem, resulting in estimates that better match system structure.<ref name="Tibshirani 2005">{{Cite journal |last1=Tibshirani |first1=Robert |last2=Saunders |first2=Michael |last3=Rosset |first3=Saharon |last4=Zhu |first4=Ji |last5=Knight |first5=Keith |date=2005 |title=Sparsity and Smoothness via the Fused Lasso |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3647602 |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Statistical Methodology) |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=91–108 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9868.2005.00490.x |jstor=3647602 |issn=1369-7412|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Lasso-regularized models can be fit using techniques including [[subgradient methods]], [[least-angle regression]] (LARS), and [[proximal gradient methods]]. Determining the optimal value for the regularization parameter is an important part of ensuring that the model performs well; it is typically chosen using [[cross-validation (statistics)|cross-validation]].

=== Elastic net ===
{{Main|Elastic net regularization}}

In 2005, Zou and Hastie introduced the [[Elastic net regularization|elastic net]].<ref name = "Zou 2005" /> When ''p''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''n'' (the number of covariates is greater than the sample size) lasso can select only ''n'' covariates (even when more are associated with the outcome) and it tends to select one covariate from any set of highly correlated covariates. Additionally, even when ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''p'', ridge regression tends to perform better given strongly correlated covariates.

The elastic net extends lasso by adding an additional <math> \ell^2 </math> penalty term giving
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \left\| y - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \lambda_1 \| \beta \|_1 + \lambda_2 \| \beta \|_2^2 \right\}, </math>
which is equivalent to solving
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\min_{ \beta_0, \beta } \left\{ \left\| y - \beta_0 - X \beta \right\|_2^2 \right\} & \text{ subject to } ( 1 - \alpha ) \| \beta \|_1 + \alpha \| \beta \|_2^2 \leq t, \\
& \text{ where } \alpha = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}.
\end{align}</math>

This problem can be written in a simple lasso form
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta^* \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \left\| y^* - X^* \beta^* \right\|_2^2 + \lambda^* \| \beta^* \|_1 \right\} </math>
letting
<math display="block"> X_{(n+p) \times p}^* = ( 1 + \lambda_2 )^{-1/2} \binom{X}{ \lambda_2^{1/2} I_{p \times p} }, </math>
<math display="block"> y_{(n+p)}^* = \binom{y}{0^p}, \qquad \lambda^* = \frac{ \lambda_1 }{ \sqrt{ 1 + \lambda_2 } }, </math>
<math display="block"> \beta^* = \sqrt{ 1 + \lambda_2 } \beta. </math>

Then <math> \hat{\beta} = \frac{ \hat{\beta}^* }{ \sqrt{ 1 + \lambda_2 } } </math>, which, when the covariates are orthogonal to each other, gives
<math display="block"> \hat{\beta}_j
= \frac{ \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;*,\text{OLS}} }{ \sqrt{ 1 + \lambda_2 } } \max \Biggl( 0, 1 - \frac{ \lambda^* }{ \bigl| \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;*,\text{OLS}} \bigr| } \Biggr)
= \frac{\hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} }{ 1 + \lambda_2 } \max \Biggl( 0, 1 - \frac{ \lambda_1 }{ \bigl| \hat\beta{}_j^{\!\;\text{OLS}} \bigr| } \Biggr) = ( 1 + \lambda_2 )^{-1} \hat{\beta}{}^\text{lasso}_j.
</math>

So the result of the elastic net penalty is a combination of the effects of the lasso and ridge penalties.

Returning to the general case, the fact that the penalty function is now strictly convex means that if <math> x_{(j)} = x_{(k)} </math>, <math> \hat{\beta}_j = \hat{\beta}_k </math>, which is a change from lasso.<ref name = "Zou 2005" /> In general, if <math> \hat{\beta}_j \hat{\beta_k} > 0 </math>
<math display="block"> \frac{ | \hat{\beta}_j - \hat{\beta_k} | }{ \| y \| } \leq \lambda_2^{-1} \sqrt{ 2 ( 1 - \rho_{jk} ) }, \text{ where } \rho = X^\intercal X, </math>
is the sample correlation matrix because the <math> x </math> 's are normalized.

Therefore, highly correlated covariates tend to have similar regression coefficients, with the degree of similarity depending on both <math> \| y \|_1 </math> and <math> \lambda_2 </math>, which is different from lasso. This phenomenon, in which strongly correlated covariates have similar regression coefficients, is referred to as the grouping effect. Grouping is desirable since, in applications such as tying genes to a disease, finding all the associated covariates is preferable, rather than selecting one from each set of correlated covariates, as lasso often does.<ref name = "Zou 2005" /> In addition, selecting only one from each group typically results in increased prediction error, since the model is less robust (which is why ridge regression often outperforms lasso).

=== Group lasso ===

In 2006, Yuan and Lin introduced the group lasso to allow predefined groups of covariates to jointly be selected into or out of a model.<ref name = "Yuan 2006" /> This is useful in many settings, perhaps most obviously when a categorical variable is coded as a collection of binary covariates. In this case, group lasso can ensure that all the variables encoding the categorical covariate are included or excluded together. Another setting in which grouping is natural is in biological studies. Since genes and proteins often lie in known pathways, which pathways are related to an outcome may be more significant than whether individual genes are. The objective function for the group lasso is a natural generalization of the standard lasso objective
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \biggl\{ \biggl\| y - \sum_{j=1}^J X_j \beta_j \biggr\|_2^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^J \| \beta_j \|_{K_j} \biggr\}, \qquad \| z \|_{K_j} = ( z^\intercal K_j z )^{1/2} </math>
where the [[design matrix]] <math> X </math> and covariate vector <math> \beta </math> have been replaced by a collection of design matrices <math> X_j </math> and covariate vectors <math> \beta_j </math>, one for each of the J groups. Additionally, the penalty term is now a sum over <math> \ell^2 </math> norms defined by the positive definite matrices <math> K_j </math>. If each covariate is in its own group and <math> K_j = I </math>, then this reduces to the standard lasso, while if there is only a single group and <math> K_1 = I </math>, it reduces to ridge regression. Since the penalty reduces to an <math> \ell^2 </math> norm on the subspaces defined by each group, it cannot select out only some of the covariates from a group, just as ridge regression cannot. However, because the penalty is the sum over the different subspace norms, as in the standard lasso, the constraint has some non-differential points, which correspond to some subspaces being identically zero. Therefore, it can set the coefficient vectors corresponding to some subspaces to zero, while only shrinking others. However, it is possible to extend the group lasso to the so-called sparse group lasso, which can select individual covariates within a group, by adding an additional <math> \ell^1 </math> penalty to each group subspace.<ref name = "Puig 2009" /> Another extension, group lasso with overlap allows covariates to be shared across groups, e.g., if a gene were to occur in two pathways.<ref name = "Jacob 2009" />

The "gglasso" package by in R, allows for fast and efficient implementation of Group LASSO.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Yi |last2=Zou |first2=Hui |date=November 2015 |title=A fast unified algorithm for solving group-lasso penalize learning problems |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11222-014-9498-5 |journal=Statistics and Computing |language=en |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=1129–1141 |doi=10.1007/s11222-014-9498-5 |s2cid=255072855 |issn=0960-3174|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Fused lasso ===
In some cases, the phenomenon under study may have important spatial or temporal structure that must be considered during analysis, such as [[time series]] or image-based data. In 2005, Tibshirani and colleagues introduced the fused lasso to extend the use of lasso to this type of data.<ref name = "Tibshirani 2005" /> The fused lasso objective function is
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \min_\beta \biggl\{ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( y_i - x_i^\intercal \beta \right)^2 \biggr\} \\[4pt]
& \text{ subject to } \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|  \leq t_1 \text{ and } \sum_{j=2}^p |\beta_j - \beta_{j-1}|  \leq t_2.
\end{align}</math>

The first constraint is the lasso constraint, while the second directly penalizes large changes with respect to the temporal or spatial structure, which forces the coefficients to vary smoothly to reflect the system's underlying logic. Clustered lasso<ref name=clusteredlasso>{{cite journal|last1=She|first1=Yiyuan|title=Sparse regression with exact clustering|journal=Electronic Journal of Statistics|volume=4|pages=1055–1096|doi=10.1214/10-EJS578|year=2010|doi-access=free}}</ref> is a generalization of fused lasso that identifies and groups relevant covariates based on their effects (coefficients). The basic idea is to penalize the differences between the coefficients so that nonzero ones cluster. This can be modeled using the following regularization:
<math display="block"> \sum_{i<j}^p |\beta_i - \beta_j|  \leq t_2. </math>

In contrast, variables can be clustered into highly correlated groups, and then a single representative covariate can be extracted from each cluster.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Reid|first1=Stephen|title=Sparse regression and marginal testing using cluster prototypes|journal=Biostatistics|volume=17|issue=2|pages=364–76|date=2015|doi=10.1093/biostatistics/kxv049|pmid=26614384 | pmc=5006118|arxiv=1503.00334|bibcode=2015arXiv150300334R}}</ref>

Algorithms exist that solve the fused lasso problem, and some generalizations of it. Algorithms can solve it exactly in a finite number of operations.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bento|first1=Jose|title=On the Complexity of the Weighted Fused Lasso |journal= IEEE Signal Processing Letters|volume=25|issue=10|pages=1595–1599|date=2018|bibcode=2018ISPL...25.1595B|arxiv=1801.04987|doi=10.1109/LSP.2018.2867800|s2cid=5008891}}</ref>

=== Quasi-norms and bridge regression ===
[[File:PQSQ potential.png|120px|thumb|An example of a PQSQ (piece-wise quadratic function of subquadratic growth) potential function <math>u(x)</math>; here the majorant function is <math>f(x)=x</math>; the potential is defined with trimming after <math>r_3</math>.]]
[[File:PQSQ2.png|120px|thumb|An example how efficient PQSQ regularized regression works just as <math> \ell^1 </math>-norm lasso<ref name="EMgithub"/>]]

Lasso, elastic net, group and fused lasso construct the penalty functions from the <math> \ell^1 </math> and <math> \ell^2 </math> norms (with weights, if necessary). The bridge regression utilises general <math> \ell^p </math> norms (<math> p \geq 1 </math>) and quasinorms (<math>0< p < 1 </math>).<ref name = "Fu 1998">Fu, Wenjiang J. 1998. “[https://www.jstor.org/stable/1390712 The Bridge versus the Lasso]”. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 7 (3).  Taylor & Francis: 397-416.</ref> For example, for ''p''=1/2 the analogue of lasso objective in the Lagrangian form is to solve
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| y - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \lambda \sqrt{\| \beta \|_{1/2}} \right\}, </math>
where
<math display="block"> \| \beta \|_{1/2}=\biggl(\sum_{j=1}^p \sqrt{|\beta_j|} \biggr)^2</math>

It is claimed that the fractional quasi-norms <math> \ell^p </math> (<math>0< p < 1 </math>) provide more meaningful results in data analysis both theoretically and empirically.<ref>Aggarwal C.C., Hinneburg A., Keim D.A. (2001) "[http://kops.uni-konstanz.de/bitstream/handle/123456789/5715/On_the_Surprising_Behavior_of_Distance_Metric_in_High_Dimensional_Space.pdf?sequence=1 On the Surprising Behavior of Distance Metrics in High Dimensional Space]." In: Van den Bussche J., Vianu V. (eds) Database Theory — ICDT 2001. ICDT 2001. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Vol. 1973. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, pp. 420-434.</ref> The non-convexity of these quasi-norms complicates the [[optimization problem]]. To solve this problem, an expectation-minimization procedure is developed<ref name="GMZ2016">Gorban, A.N.; Mirkes, E.M.; Zinovyev, A. (2016) "[https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.06276 Piece-wise quadratic approximations of arbitrary error functions for fast and robust machine learning.]" Neural Networks, 84, 28-38.</ref> and implemented<ref name="EMgithub">Mirkes E.M. [https://github.com/Mirkes/PQSQ-regularized-regression/wiki PQSQ-regularized-regression repository], GitHub.</ref> for minimization of function
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| y - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \vartheta(\beta_j^2)\right\}, </math>
where <math>\vartheta(\gamma)</math> is an arbitrary concave monotonically increasing function (for example, <math>\vartheta(\gamma)=\sqrt{\gamma}</math> gives the lasso penalty and <math>\vartheta(\gamma)=\gamma^{1/4}</math> gives the <math> \ell^{1/2} </math> penalty).

The efficient algorithm for minimization is based on piece-wise [[Taylor's theorem|quadratic approximation]] of subquadratic growth (PQSQ).<ref name="GMZ2016"/>

=== Adaptive lasso ===

The adaptive lasso was introduced by Zou in 2006 for linear regression<ref name="Zou2006"/> and by Zhang and Lu in 2007 for proportional hazards regression.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=H. H. |last2=Lu |first2=W. |date=2007-08-05 |title=Adaptive Lasso for Cox's proportional hazards model |url=https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/biomet/asm037 |journal=Biometrika |language=en |volume=94 |issue=3 |pages=691–703 |doi=10.1093/biomet/asm037 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Prior lasso ===

The prior lasso was introduced for generalized linear models by Jiang et al. in 2016 to incorporate prior information, such as the importance of certain covariates.<ref name=priorlasso>{{cite journal|last1=Jiang|first1=Yuan|title=Variable selection with prior information for generalized linear models via the prior lasso method|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=111|issue=513|pages=355–376|doi=10.1080/01621459.2015.1008363|pmid=27217599|pmc=4874534|year=2016}}</ref> In prior lasso, such information is summarized into pseudo responses (called prior responses) <math> \hat{y}^{\mathrm{p}} </math> and then an additional criterion function is added to the usual objective function with a lasso penalty. [[Without loss of generality]], in linear regression, the new objective function can be written as
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| y - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \frac{1}{N} \eta \left\| \hat{y}^{\mathrm{p}} - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|_{1} \right\}, </math>
which is equivalent to
<math display="block"> \min_{ \beta \in \mathbb{R}^p } \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \left\| \tilde{y} - X \beta \right\|_2^2 + \frac{\lambda}{1 + \eta} \| \beta \|_{1} \right\}, </math>

the usual lasso objective function with the responses <math> y </math> being replaced by a weighted average of the observed responses and the prior responses <math> \tilde{y} =  (y + \eta\hat{y}^{\mathrm{p}}) / (1 + \eta) </math> (called the adjusted response values by the prior information).

In prior lasso, the parameter <math> \eta </math> is called a balancing parameter, in that it balances the relative importance of the data and the prior information. In the extreme case of <math> \eta = 0 </math>, prior lasso is reduced to lasso. If <math> \eta = \infty </math>, prior lasso will solely rely on the prior information to fit the model. Furthermore, the balancing parameter <math> \eta </math> has another appealing interpretation: it controls the variance of <math> \beta </math> in its prior distribution from a Bayesian viewpoint.

Prior lasso is more efficient in parameter estimation and prediction (with a smaller estimation error and prediction error) when the prior information is of high quality, and is robust to the low quality prior information with a good choice of the balancing parameter <math> \eta </math>.

=== Ensemble lasso ===

Lasso can be run in an [[Ensemble learning|ensemble]]. This can be especially useful when the data is high-dimensional. The procedure involves running lasso on each of several random subsets of the data and collating the results.<ref>D. Amaratunga, J. Cabrera, Y. Cherckas, and Y. Lee (2011). Ensemble classifiers. doi: 10.1214/11-IMSCOLL816.</ref><ref>D. Urda, L. Franco and J. M. Jerez (2017), Classification of high dimensional data using LASSO ensembles, IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (SSCI), pp. 1-7, doi: 10.1109/SSCI.2017.8280875.</ref><ref>O. Samarawickrama, R. Jayatillake, and D. Amaratunga (2022) Identifying Ordinal Nature Inherited Proteins Associated with a Certain Disease, SLIIT Journal of Humanities and Sciences, 3(1), p. 37-45. doi: 10.4038/sjhs.v3i1.49.</ref>

== Computing lasso solutions ==
{{main|Proximal gradient methods for learning#Lasso regularization}}
The loss function of the lasso is not differentiable, but a wide variety of techniques from convex analysis and optimization theory have been developed to compute the solutions path of the lasso. These include [[coordinate descent]],<ref name="Friedman 20102">Jerome Friedman, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani. 2010. “Regularization Paths for Generalized Linear Models via Coordinate Descent”. Journal of Statistical Software 33 (1): 1-21. https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v033i01/v33i01.pdf.</ref> subgradient methods, [[least-angle regression]] (LARS),<ref name="Efron 20042">{{Cite journal |last1=Efron |first1=Bradley |last2=Hastie |first2=Trevor |last3=Johnstone |first3=Iain |last4=Tibshirani |first4=Robert |date=2004 |title=Least Angle Regression |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3448465 |journal=The Annals of Statistics |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=407–451 |doi=10.1214/009053604000000067 |jstor=3448465 |issn=0090-5364|arxiv=math/0406456 }}</ref> and proximal gradient methods. [[Subderivative|Subgradient]] methods are the natural generalization of traditional methods such as [[gradient descent]] and [[stochastic gradient descent]] to the case in which the objective function is not differentiable at all points. LARS is a method that is closely tied to lasso models, and in many cases allows them to be fit efficiently, though it may not perform well in all circumstances. LARS generates complete solution paths.<ref name="Efron 20042" /> Proximal methods have become popular because of their flexibility and performance and are an area of active research. The choice of method will depend on the particular lasso variant, the data and the available resources. However, proximal methods generally perform well.

The "glmnet" package in R, where "glm" is a reference to "generalized linear models" and "net" refers to the "net" from "elastic net" provides an extremely efficient way to implement LASSO and some of its variants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Friedman |first1=Jerome |last2=Hastie |first2=Trevor |last3=Tibshirani |first3=Robert |date=2010 |title=Regularization Paths for Generalized Linear Models via Coordinate Descent |journal=Journal of Statistical Software |language=en |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=1–22 |doi=10.18637/jss.v033.i01  |pmid=20808728 |pmc=2929880 |issn=1548-7660|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Simon |first1=Noah |last2=Friedman |first2=Jerome |last3=Hastie |first3=Trevor |last4=Tibshirani |first4=Rob |date=2011 |title=Regularization Paths for Cox's Proportional Hazards Model via Coordinate Descent |journal=Journal of Statistical Software |language=en |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.18637/jss.v039.i05  |doi-access=free|issn=1548-7660 |pmc=4824408 |pmid=27065756}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tay |first1=J. Kenneth |last2=Narasimhan |first2=Balasubramanian |last3=Hastie |first3=Trevor |date=2023 |title=Elastic Net Regularization Paths for All Generalized Linear Models |journal=Journal of Statistical Software |language=en |volume=106 |issue=1 |doi=10.18637/jss.v106.i01  |pmid=37138589 |pmc=10153598 |issn=1548-7660|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The "celer" package in Python provides a highly efficient solver for the Lasso problem, often outperforming traditional solvers like [[scikit-learn]] by up to 100 times in certain scenarios, particularly with high-dimensional datasets. This package leverages dual extrapolation techniques to achieve its performance gains.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Massias |first1=Mathurin |last2=Gramfort |first2=Alexandre |last3=Salmon |first3=Joseph |date=2018 |title=Celer: a Fast Solver for the Lasso with Dual Extrapolation |journal=Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning |volume=80 |pages=3321–3330 |arxiv=1802.07481 |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/massias18a/massias18a.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Massias |first1=Mathurin |last2=Vaiter |first2=Samuel |last3=Gramfort |first3=Alexandre |last4=Salmon |first4=Joseph |date=2020 |title=Dual Extrapolation for Sparse GLMs |journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research |volume=21 |issue=234 |pages=1–33 |url=http://jmlr.org/papers/v21/19-587.html }}</ref> The celer package is available at [https://github.com/mathurinm/celer GitHub].

== Choice of regularization parameter ==
Choosing the regularization parameter (<math>\lambda</math>) is a fundamental part of lasso. A good value is essential to the performance of lasso since it controls the strength of shrinkage and variable selection, which, in moderation can improve both prediction accuracy and interpretability. However, if the regularization becomes too strong, important variables may be omitted and coefficients may be shrunk excessively, which can harm both predictive capacity and inferencing. [[Cross-validation (statistics)|Cross-validation]] is often used to find the regularization parameter.

Information criteria such as the [[Bayesian information criterion]] (BIC) and the [[Akaike information criterion]] (AIC) might be preferable to cross-validation, because they are faster to compute and their performance is less volatile in small samples.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Science: Under Submission|last=Hoornweg|first=Victor|publisher=Hoornweg Press|year=2018|isbn=978-90-829188-0-9|chapter=Chapter 9|chapter-url=http://www.victorhoornweg.com}}</ref> An information criterion selects the estimator's regularization parameter by maximizing a model's in-sample accuracy while penalizing its effective number of parameters/degrees of freedom. Zou et al. proposed to measure the effective degrees of freedom by counting the number of parameters that deviate from zero.<ref name="Zou 20052">{{cite journal|last1=Zou|first1=Hui|last2=Hastie|first2=Trevor|last3=Tibshirani|first3=Robert|year=2007|title=On the 'Degrees of Freedom' of the Lasso|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=35|issue=5|pages=2173–2792|doi=10.1214/009053607000000127|doi-access=free|arxiv=0712.0881}}</ref> The degrees of freedom approach was considered flawed by Kaufman and Rosset<ref name="KaufmanRosset2014">{{cite journal|last1=Kaufman|first1=S.|last2=Rosset|first2=S.|title=When does more regularization imply fewer degrees of freedom? Sufficient conditions and counterexamples|journal=Biometrika|volume=101|issue=4|year=2014|pages=771–784|issn=0006-3444|doi=10.1093/biomet/asu034}}</ref> and Janson et al.,<ref name="JansonFithian2015">{{cite journal|last1=Janson|first1=Lucas|last2=Fithian|first2=William|last3=Hastie|first3=Trevor J.|title=Effective degrees of freedom: a flawed metaphor|journal=Biometrika|volume=102|issue=2|year=2015|pages=479–485|issn=0006-3444|doi=10.1093/biomet/asv019|pmid=26977114|pmc=4787623}}</ref> because a model's degrees of freedom might increase even when it is penalized harder by the regularization parameter. As an alternative, the relative simplicity measure defined above can be used to count the effective number of parameters.<ref name=":0" /> For the lasso, this measure is given by
<math display="block">\hat{\mathcal{P}} = \sum_{i=1}^p  \frac{|\beta_i-\beta_{0,i}|}{\frac{1}{p} \sum_{l} |b_{\text{OLS},l}-\beta_{0,l}|},</math>
which monotonically increases from zero to <math> p </math> as the regularization parameter decreases from <math> \infty </math> to zero.

== Selected applications ==

LASSO has been applied in economics and finance, and was found to improve prediction and to select sometimes neglected variables, for example in corporate bankruptcy prediction literature,<ref name="Tian">{{cite journal|last1=Shaonan|first1=Tian|last2=Yu|first2=Yan |last3=Guo|first3=Hui |year=2015|title=Variable selection and corporate bankruptcy forecasts|journal=Journal of Banking & Finance|volume=52|issue=1|pages=89–100|doi=10.1016/j.jbankfin.2014.12.003|doi-access=}}</ref> or high growth firms prediction.<ref name="sbe">{{cite journal|last1=Coad|first1=Alex|last2=Srhoj|first2=Stjepan |year=2020|title=Catching Gazelles with a Lasso: Big data techniques for the prediction of high-growth firms|journal= Small Business Economics |volume=55|issue=1|pages=541–565|doi=10.1007/s11187-019-00203-3|s2cid=255011751 |doi-access=}}</ref>
